These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Here, **camp** represents the army that has camped in a place. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the army of the Philistines]

x.ASV: And David did so, as Jehovah commanded him, and smote the Philistines from Geba until thou come to Gezer.

x.YLT: And David doth so, as Jehovah commanded him, and smiteth the Philistines from Geba unto thy coming to Gazer.

nt: The Septuagint (an ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible) and the parallel passage in [1 Chronicles 14:16](../../1ch/14/16.md) read “Gibeon” instead of **Geba**. That may have been the original reading, particularly since the location of Gibeon suits the account of this battle better than the location of Geba. At one point in the process of transmission, scribes may have left out the additional letters that would have spelled “Gibeon” rather than “Geba,” either accidentally or as a way of abbreviating. If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT.
